siem-brute-force.title: RDP Brute Force Detection
siem-brute-force.description: Analyze SIEM alerts to identify a brute force attempt on the RDP service. Triage alerts and determine the incident severity.
siem-brute-force.q1: What is the nature of alert ID-001?
siem-brute-force.q1_exp: The 847 failed login attempts from an external IP within 12 minutes clearly indicate a brute force attack. The pattern is characteristic: same source IP, rapid attempts, multiple targeted accounts.
siem-brute-force.q2: What severity level would you assign to this incident?
siem-brute-force.q2_exp: Severity HIGH: the attack is active and targets a remote access service (RDP), but no successful connections have been detected. If a connection had succeeded, it would be CRITICAL.
siem-brute-force.q3: What action do you recommend as a priority?
siem-brute-force.q3_opt1: Block the source IP at the firewall
siem-brute-force.q3_exp: The priority is to block the source IP at the firewall to stop the attack immediately. Then verify that no accounts have been compromised and document the incident.
siem-brute-force.q4: What IOCs should you extract from this incident?
siem-brute-force.q4_exp: All IOCs are important: the source IP (for blocking and TI sharing), targeted accounts (to check if compromised), and timestamps (for correlation with other events).

phishing-ceo-fraud.title: Phishing — CEO Fraud
phishing-ceo-fraud.description: Analyze a suspicious email claiming to be from the company CEO. Examine headers and content to identify phishing indicators.
phishing-ceo-fraud.q1: The SPF header shows 'softfail'. What does this mean?
phishing-ceo-fraud.q1_opt1: The sending server is not authorized but the domain tolerates relay
phishing-ceo-fraud.q1_exp: An SPF 'softfail' (~all) means the sending server is not explicitly authorized by the domain's SPF record, but the domain does not firmly reject these emails. It's a potential spoofing indicator.
phishing-ceo-fraud.q2: What is the most critical phishing indicator in this email?
phishing-ceo-fraud.q2_opt1: The Reply-To address differs from the From address
phishing-ceo-fraud.q2_opt3: The email was sent at 2 PM
phishing-ceo-fraud.q2_exp: A different Reply-To from the From address is a strong technical phishing/BEC indicator. The attacker wants replies to go to an address they control, not the real CEO's address.
phishing-ceo-fraud.q3: Which MITRE ATT&CK technique corresponds to this attack?
phishing-ceo-fraud.q3_exp: This attack uses T1566.002 (Spearphishing Link) because the email contains a fraudulent link redirecting to a fake portal. There is no malicious attachment, which excludes T1566.001.

network-c2-beacon.title: C2 Beaconing Detection
network-c2-beacon.description: Analyze network traffic to identify a Command & Control (C2) communication pattern. Examine suspicious flows and identify the malware.
network-c2-beacon.q1: What traffic pattern indicates C2 beaconing?
network-c2-beacon.q1_opt1: Regular outbound connections to the same IP every 60 seconds
network-c2-beacon.q1_exp: C2 beaconing is characterized by outbound connections at regular intervals (here every ~60 seconds) to the same IP/domain. This regularity (low jitter) is a strong indicator of automated communication with a C2 server.
network-c2-beacon.q2: What port is used by the C2 to avoid detection?
network-c2-beacon.q2_opt1: 443 (HTTPS) — encrypted traffic blending with legitimate traffic
network-c2-beacon.q2_exp: Port 443 (HTTPS) is commonly used by modern C2s because encrypted traffic blends with legitimate web traffic, making signature-based detection impossible. The content is masked by TLS.

incident-ransomware.title: Ransomware Incident Response
incident-ransomware.description: Ransomware has been detected on the network. Reconstruct the kill chain, make containment decisions and document the incident.
incident-ransomware.q1: What is the first action to take?
incident-ransomware.q1_opt1: Isolate infected machines from the network
incident-ransomware.q1_opt4: Send an email to all employees
incident-ransomware.q1_exp: Network isolation is the absolute priority to prevent lateral spread of the ransomware. Never pay the ransom as a first step and never format machines before collecting forensic evidence.
incident-ransomware.q2_exp: The typical ransomware kill chain: 1) Initial phishing 2) Payload execution 3) Persistence 4) Internal reconnaissance 5) Lateral movement 6) Data exfiltration 7) File encryption.

malware-trojan.title: Banking Trojan Analysis
malware-trojan.description: An endpoint has been flagged for suspicious behavior. Analyze the IOCs, malware behavior and classify the threat.
malware-trojan.q1: What type of malware matches this behavior?
malware-trojan.q1_exp: The observed characteristics (browser injection, banking form interception, targeted keylogging on financial sites) are typical of a Banking Trojan like Emotet or TrickBot.

sigma-detection.title: SIGMA Rule Creation
sigma-detection.description: From the provided logs, identify malicious patterns and validate the corresponding SIGMA rules.
sigma-detection.q1: Which SIGMA rule correctly detects encoded PowerShell execution?
sigma-detection.q1_exp: Detecting encoded PowerShell execution relies on the command line containing the flags '-enc', '-encodedcommand', or '-e' followed by a Base64 string. This is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001.

threat-intel-apt.title: APT Attribution and Threat Intelligence
threat-intel-apt.description: Analyze IOCs from an attack campaign and map them to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Identify the potential APT group.
threat-intel-apt.q1: Which APT group matches these TTPs?
threat-intel-apt.q1_exp: The observed TTPs (supply chain compromise, SUNBURST backdoor usage, DNS C2, targeting government organizations) match the profile of APT29 (Cozy Bear), linked to Russian intelligence services (SVR).
